title: Pressure-cooker chicken soup
subtitle: A restorative bowl in 25 minutes
excerpt: Chicken thighs simmered under pressure with aromatics, carrot, and celery into a rich, clear broth. Quick-cooked but truly nourishing, the kind of soup that earns its reputation.
sourceNotes: Chicken soup as a restorative dish appears across almost every culinary tradition, Jewish chicken broth, French pot-au-feu, Vietnamese pho, Chinese congee all derive from the same principle of simmering a bird in water until the liquid becomes nourishing. The pressure cooker compresses the usual 2-hour simmer.

recipe.freezeNotes: Cool and freeze in airtight containers for up to 4 months. Add noodles or pasta fresh after reheating.
recipe.batchNotes: Double easily and freeze in individual portions.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The soup is better the next day. Refrigerate for up to 3 days. Add any starch component fresh when reheating.

content.text: Pressure-cooker chicken soup produces a broth with real depth in 20 minutes at pressure, clear, golden, and properly flavoured. The chicken thighs shred into the soup after cooking, and the vegetables soften without becoming waterlogged. It is faster than any other method that produces a result this good.

Bone-in chicken thighs give the best result because the bone contributes gelatin to the broth, giving it body. Boneless thighs also work but produce a slightly thinner broth. The skins add flavour and fat; remove them if you prefer a cleaner, lighter soup.

Add noodles or small pasta shapes directly to the finished soup and simmer for a few minutes until cooked through. These are best added fresh to each serving rather than cooked into the main batch, they absorb liquid quickly and go soft in storage.

Put the chicken thighs, carrot, celery, onion, garlic, thyme, and bay leaf in the pressure cooker. Pour in {{stock-chicken}} of chicken stock. Season with salt and pepper. Seal the lid and bring to high pressure. Cook at high pressure for 20 minutes. Allow a natural pressure release of 10 minutes, then quick-release.
Lift out the chicken thighs. Discard the thyme and bay. Shred the chicken into strips with two forks and return to the soup. Taste and adjust the seasoning. Bring back to a simmer to heat through.

rows.cause: A rolling boil during pressure building can cloud the broth.
rows.fix: This does not affect the flavour. For a clear broth next time, allow the pot to reach pressure gently over low heat.

rows.cause: Pressure cooking breaks down vegetables quickly.
rows.fix: Reduce cooking time to 15 minutes for firmer vegetables, or add fresh sliced carrot and celery to the finished soup and simmer for 5 minutes in the open pot.

rows.cause: The stock was weak, or too much water was added.
rows.fix: Season generously and stir through a teaspoon of soy sauce or fish sauce to add depth without making it taste of either ingredient.

content.text: This soup is particularly good as a large batch frozen in individual portions. Defrost overnight in the fridge, reheat in a saucepan, and add a handful of noodles or small pasta to cook in the hot broth for the last few minutes.

Chicken soup has a reputation as a restorative food across cultures. Whether or not it is medicinal, it is undeniably warming, nourishing, and straightforward, the kind of thing you make when someone is unwell or when the weather has been bad for a week. The pressure-cooker version gives you the depth of a long-simmered broth without the two-hour wait.
